title: Network automation script that builds a device report
summary: A Python tool that collects data from network devices over SSH with Netmiko or over RESTCONF, parses it into structured data and writes an inventory and health report.
why: Automation is on the CCNA blueprint and in many network job postings. A working script that turns show commands or API calls into a clean report proves you can bridge networking and code, a valuable mix for junior candidates.
brief:
Write a Python tool that reads an inventory file (YAML) of devices, connects to each one, gathers data and produces a report: hostname, model, software version, uptime, interface status (up, down, administratively down) and a few health checks, such as interfaces with input errors, unused ports that are not shut down, or OSPF neighbors that are not FULL. Output a Markdown or HTML report, a CSV, and a JSON file with the structured data.

You need devices that accept real SSH or API connections, which Packet Tracer does not offer to an outside Python script. Use Cisco Modeling Labs (its free edition allows a small lab, enough for a few routers and switches), a Cisco DevNet sandbox (Cisco has offered always-on and reservable IOS XE sandboxes; check the current list), or virtual router images you are licensed to run. Then choose a collection path: Netmiko over SSH, sending show commands and parsing the output with TextFSM templates (ntc-templates) or Genie; or RESTCONF on IOS XE, requesting YANG-modeled data as JSON over HTTPS.

Constraints: credentials come from environment variables or a prompt, never the repository. Devices are polled concurrently with a sensible limit. An unreachable device is reported and skipped, never crashing the run. Parsing functions are unit tested against saved sample output, so tests run without any devices. The tool is read-only: it collects and reports and never changes configuration (configuration backup is a good stretch goal).

milestones.title: Lab and access
tasks: Build a lab of at least three devices in Cisco Modeling Labs, or reserve a DevNet sandbox
Enable SSH (and RESTCONF if you use it) with a dedicated low-privilege user
Connect once by hand with ssh or curl to confirm access
milestones.doneWhen: You can log in to every device over SSH (or get a RESTCONF response) from the machine that will run the script.

milestones.title: Inventory and first connection
tasks: Write an inventory YAML file with device names, addresses and platform types
Connect to one device with Netmiko (or requests for RESTCONF) and print show version
milestones.doneWhen: Running the script prints one device's hostname and software version, and no credentials are stored in the repository.

milestones.title: Parsing into structured data
tasks: Parse show version and show ip interface brief (or the RESTCONF interface data) into Python dictionaries
Save raw sample outputs as test fixtures
Unit test the parsers with pytest against the fixtures
milestones.doneWhen: `pytest` passes with no devices reachable, and the parsed data includes every interface with its status.

milestones.title: All devices, safely
tasks: Poll the inventory with a thread pool and a concurrency limit
Catch timeouts and authentication failures per device and record them
Log progress and print a summary at the end
milestones.doneWhen: With one device powered off, the run still completes, reports that device as unreachable and includes data for the others.

milestones.title: Report and health checks
tasks: Write the Markdown or HTML report, the CSV and the JSON data file
Add at least three health checks
List failed checks at the top of the report
milestones.doneWhen: One command produces all three output files, and a deliberately misconfigured device shows up as a failed check.

milestones.title: Document and demo
tasks: A README with setup, the lab description, usage and a sample report
A short GIF or screenshot of a run and its report
A section on limitations and next steps
milestones.doneWhen: A reviewer can read a sample report in the repository and follow the README to run the tool against their own lab.

stretch: Back up running configurations to dated files and show a diff between runs
Add a RESTCONF collector alongside Netmiko and compare the two
Do the same job with an Ansible playbook and compare it with your script
Schedule nightly runs and keep a history of changes
rubric: A reviewer should find no credentials in the repository or its history
A reviewer should see an inventory file and code that handles any number of devices
A reviewer should see parsed, structured data in the report rather than pasted screen output
A reviewer should see unit tests for the parsers that run without network devices
A reviewer should see an unreachable device reported without crashing the run
A reviewer should see a sample report with at least three meaningful health checks
A reviewer should see a README that explains the lab setup and how to run the tool
showcase: Create a GitHub repository with the code, a sample inventory using fake addresses, test fixtures, a sample report and a GIF of a run
Put a screenshot of the report and a small lab topology diagram at the top of the README
Explain your choice of Netmiko or RESTCONF in a short design section
Feature it on your resume for network, operations and DevOps-flavored roles alike
resumeBullet: Wrote a Python tool (Netmiko, TextFSM) that inventories Cisco IOS devices concurrently, parses show output into structured data and generates Markdown and CSV health reports; parsers covered by pytest fixtures, credentials kept out of code.
interviewTalkingPoints: Screen scraping with Netmiko versus structured data from RESTCONF and YANG: the trade-offs
How you handled unreachable devices, timeouts and bad credentials
How you tested parsing code without real devices
Why the tool is read-only, and how you would add configuration changes safely
What you would automate next on a real network team
